restatement.intent: Describe each operation of an engine exactly once, as a data record, and let every consumer — checker, help, refusals, agent context, tests — read that record instead of keeping its own copy.
restatement.problem: When several consumers each hold their own idea of what an operation accepts and returns, they drift apart, and the caller gets silent wrong behaviour instead of a precise refusal.
restatement.solution: Register one OpRecord per (receiver kind, name), holding arguments with type, unit, default, hard limits, usual range and redirects, plus a cross-argument hook, result kind and fields, flags, docs and an implementation or expansion. Registration validates records structurally and semantically; the binder checks calls against the record, the describer renders help from it, the diagnoser builds refusals from it, and a walker test calls every record and compares results with declared fields. Anything that cannot be a record goes on one visible exception list with its own test.

quiz.answer: The call binds successfully and returns the bound call carrying a Warning(RANGE, spec, usualHint); defaults never warn, only caller-supplied values. That warning must be copied into the reply the caller reads — a warning that reaches only a log is no warning.
quiz.where: Implementation note 2 (Separate hard limits from usual ranges); Collaborations 4; the bind pseudocode

quiz.answer: The walker test (goja-cv's TestRegistryWalk plus TestSchemaProperty), reinforced by registration: if samples live in the record, registration can refuse a callable record without them; the walk then calls every record and asserts result keys ⊆ declared fields and required fields ⊆ result keys. The chapter notes goja-cv keeps samples in the test file, which is exactly why its registration cannot enforce this.
quiz.where: Implementation note 5 (Walk the whole registry); Structure/Walker; the walker pseudocode

quiz.answer: Because goja-cv keeps its method, help and look redirects in three tables outside the registry, so a redirect added to one is invisible to the others — which is the very drift the pattern exists to prevent. Redirects are operation knowledge and belong with the operation record.
quiz.where: Implementation note 4 (Keep every near-miss redirect in the records)

quiz.answer: Any two of: binder (checks calls, produces warnings), describer (agent context line and full help), diagnoser (refusals with valid names, nearest name, fix), walker test, and the tool-schema renderer named in note 6.

transfer.why: Three independent consumers (LLM tool schema, mobile control UI, hub-side validation) plus third-party plug-ins adding actions at run time is precisely the applicability case; a function signature per plug-in cannot serve the tool schema or the control layout.

participants.Operation record: One record per action per device kind: set_temperature(on: Thermostat), dim_lights(on: Dimmer), lock_door(on: Lock), run_scene(on: Hub), plus returns and flags.
participants.Argument spec: e.g. temperature: number, unit °C, min 5, max 30, usual [16, 24], valueDocs for mode enums; scene: enumeration with value docs; duration/transition in seconds.
participants.Flags: confirm for lock_door and any irreversible action — the host sets it and a plug-in record cannot lower it; internal for actions the voice assistant must not see; identity for no-op-friendly settings.
participants.Registry: The hub's action registry, populated at start-up by core and by each device plug-in, keyed by (device kind, action name).
participants.Binder: The hub's command validator: unknown keys, types, hard limits, cross-argument hook (target temperature vs mode), warnings.
participants.Describer: Two renderings: the LLM tool description (JSON-schema-ish) and the mobile control layout (a control per argument, from type + limits + valueDocs).
participants.Diagnoser: The refusal sent back to voice/LLM or app: valid action names, nearest name, redirects (`set_temp` → `set_temperature`), clamp fix for out-of-range temperature.
participants.Walker: A plug-in conformance test that binds each record with its samples against a simulated device and checks result fields.

transfer.sketch:
-- core + each device plug-in, at start-up
registry.register(OpRecord(name: "lock_door", on: Lock, returns: Ack,
    args: [ArgSpec(name: "timeout", type: seconds, unit: s, default: 30, min: 0, max: 300, usual: [5, 60])],
    flags: { class: actuator, confirm: required },   -- host-owned, plug-in cannot lower
    redirects: [{ from: "unlock", call: "lock_door({ locked: false })" }],
    samples: { timeout: 30 }, run: plugIn.lockDoor))
registry.finishStartUp()   -- cross-record checks: redirect targets and confirm policy

bind(Lock, "lock_door", raw) → BoundCall(rec, args, warnings) | Failure
  -- same as chapter: unknown keys first, no coercion, units still as written
explain(failure, registry) → Refusal        -- feeds the tool reply and the app toast
contextLine(rec) → tool schema entry / control spec
key_notes: Note 1: plug-ins register late, so cross-record checks (redirect targets, target actions from another plug-in) must run once registration is complete, at end of start-up — not per record.

Note 6: device plug-ins will add argument types (colour temperature, scene ids, device references) faster than the core can grow; make types pluggable with accept/check/describe before that happens, and keep the tool-schema and UI consumers as modules outside the core.
Note 2 and Chapter 2: temperature is the classic unit trap — hard limits and usual ranges must be declared in °C or °F and converted only at evaluation, never at bind time.
Flags portfolio (confirm): lock_door and unlock must be confirmable and a third-party record must not be able to clear the flag; a non-interactive voice run refuses outright.
Note 8: plug-ins rename actions; a rename needs a redirect from the old name so voice transcripts still work, and a changed default changes saved routines, so defaults are part of identity.

Note 9: whatever cannot be a record (session open, device discovery, run_scene if it bypasses the action path) belongs on one exception list with a test that every name reachable from the assistant is accounted for.
transfer.risk: Treating plug-in records as trusted: a plug-in can declare confirm:false on an irreversible door action, invent units the binder cannot convert, or collide with a core action name, so the validated registry becomes the new source of silent wrong behaviour. The host needs an admission policy (confirm floor, allowed types/units, name namespace) enforced at registration.

transfer.why: The chapter's own exclusion applies: the platform already gives you the records — protobuf plus field-constraint annotations already generate clients, docs and server-side validation. A second Go registry would be a parallel source of truth and would drift from the .proto, recreating the exact problem the pattern solves. The right move is to add consumers over the existing descriptors (a doc/help renderer, an agent tool-schema generator reading descriptors and annotations), not a new registry.
key_notes: Applicability, third 'do not use it' bullet: use the typed RPC schema as the registry instead of building a parallel one.
Variations, schema-first records: if anything is missing, extend the .proto or its annotations, since that file already is the reviewable, language-neutral record.
Consequence 'generated help is flat' still applies — the gap a Go registry would seem to fill (prose help) is a Chapter 12 problem, not a registry problem.
transfer.risk: Building it anyway 'just for help text', then discovering validation and docs disagree with the generated ones; or hand-writing the operation list in Go and letting it rot as methods are added.

review_notes.note: The bolded Solution is one triple-nested sentence that lists the entire record shape, then the entire consumer set, then the exception rule. A reader cannot hold it after one pass, which is bad for the one paragraph meant to be remembered.
review_notes.suggestion: Split into three short paragraphs or a numbered list: (1) what the record contains, (2) who reads it, (3) the exception rule. Move the record field list to the Sketch, where it already exists.

review_notes.note: The sketch lists 'redirect targets exist' and 'default within limits' as semantic checks in register(), but note 1 says goja-cv's Register does not check them and that they belong to the pattern. The chapter presents a pseudocode contract the running example does not meet without saying which one is normative.
review_notes.suggestion: State the required check set once, then say plainly: goja-cv implements the structural half only; that gap is a bug in goja-cv, not an option in the pattern. Keep the sketch as the contract.

review_notes.note: Two redirect mechanisms appear with no rule separating them: record-level `redirects` on OpRecord and `registry.redirectFor(on, name)` in the diagnoser, while argument specs carry option-level redirects. Note 4 says method-level ones 'live in the operation record or the registry' — 'or' is the ambiguity.
review_notes.suggestion: Say when a redirect must be on the record (it is about that operation) versus in the registry (it is about the namespace or the help system), and give one example of each.

review_notes.note: Four of the six listed flags (pixel/geometric/decoration class, `global`, identity predicate, lossless-preview hint) are named but never explained: which consumer acts on them and what it does. Only `internal` and the hypothetical `confirm` get any prose.
review_notes.suggestion: Give one line per flag: reader, meaning, effect. Drop the ones this chapter does not use, since flags without consumers are indistinguishable from decoration.

review_notes.note: Results are described as a kind plus `fields(boundArgs) → [FieldSpec]`, but the walker only checks key presence ('nothing undeclared, nothing missing') — never a field's type, unit or nullability. Nothing says whether FieldSpec has a type at all, so the chapter's own test cannot catch a column that silently changes from count to fraction.
review_notes.suggestion: Define FieldSpec (name, type, unit, optional) and have the walker assert value kinds too; say explicitly that value-level correctness needs per-operation tests beyond the walk.

review_notes.note: The `validate?(args)` hook is acknowledged as where table-unfittable rules go, but nothing reconciles that with 'help is generated from records': a constraint living in a hook is invisible to the describer, the tool schema and the agent's context. The same applies to the `expand` graphs.
review_notes.suggestion: Require the hook to carry a machine-readable description (code, message, involved arg names) so the describer and diagnoser can render it, and say what the describer prints for hook-only rules.

review_notes.note: Third-party and user-defined operations are invited (note 10, Applicability 'by users at run time'), but the chapter never states the admission rules: who wins on a (kind, name) collision between core and plug-in, whether a plug-in may lower a host-owned flag, or which argument types a plug-in may introduce. `(on, name) unique` covers the collision by failing registration, which for a late plug-in means the hub may not start.
review_notes.suggestion: Add a note on namespacing and precedence (plug-in records are namespaced and refused, not merged, on collision) and on which flags only the host may set.

review_notes.note: `fix: clamp(failure.value, failure.spec)` is shown without saying whether anything applies it. Silently clamping contradicts the chapter's own 'strictness' force and 'nothing falls back to a default silently' (note 3); the reader cannot tell whether the fix is a suggestion to the caller or an automatic repair.
review_notes.suggestion: Say once that `fix` is always a suggested call for the caller to make (or re-issue), never an applied repair, and that the original value is quoted in the refusal.

review_notes.note: The same two anecdotes (goja-cv v1's `cv.open` encoding bug, the Editor lab's hand-written reference) are told in Motivation and re-told in four notes. Each note also spends words on what goja-cv failed to do, so the reusable rule is buried in a defect report.
review_notes.suggestion: Tell each anecdote once in Motivation and let the notes state the rule first, with a one-clause pointer to the example; cut 'goja-cv does not do X' where the sketch already shows X.

review_notes.note: 'Build the registry when a second independent consumer exists' is the only trigger given, with no sense of the cost being weighed — while the running example is sixty operations with five consumers and the chapter elsewhere says any new operation now touches shared code.
review_notes.suggestion: Add one clause on scale: a second consumer justifies the pattern, but the binder's type system is the cost, so keep the type set small until a real operation needs a new one.

ratings.comment: The core shape (record → binder/describer/diagnoser/walker) is genuinely transferable and the exclusions are well judged, but the overstuffed Solution paragraph, the two-route redirect story and the undefined flags/result-field types leave real ambiguity for anyone building it.
